control_ladder.note_beginner: Spittlebugs build up on the weeds around a planting and move onto lavender from there, so clear that weedy ground in spring. Cutting weeds that already carry foam, while the insects inside them are still young, is the one preventive step worth doing.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: This is a timed clearance, not general tidiness. UC IPM's instruction is to cut spittlebug-infested weeds in spring before the insects mature and spread, and University of Minnesota Extension's is to keep weeds down near the garden; the surrounding cover is the reservoir, and once the adults are mobile it has already emptied onto whatever grows beside it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the froth bothers you, a forceful stream from the hose washes the young insects off the stems. This is a tidying choice rather than a treatment, because an established lavender is not being harmed either way.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A hard jet takes the foam and the nymph inside it off the stem, and that is the whole effect; the feeding itself costs an established subshrub nothing. Weigh it against simply leaving them: the masses are a late-spring event that passes on its own, and the Royal Horticultural Society asks gardeners not to remove these insects at all.

control_ladder.note_beginner: On a few stems you can wipe the foam away and lift the small insect out by hand. It is slower than the hose, but it leaves the foliage dry.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Hand removal suits a handful of shoots or a small planting and is the option that does not wet the canopy. There is one generation a year in colder regions and at most two in mild ones, so a single walk through the planting in late spring usually finishes the job.

prevention_seasoned.new: There is a published prevention step, and it is weed management on a spring clock: UC IPM advises cutting spittlebug-infested weeds before the insects mature and spread, and University of Minnesota Extension advises removing weeds near the garden. The weedy cover around a planting is the reservoir the nymphs arrive from.
prevention_seasoned.why: The old text asserted 'No specific prevention is warranted.' and then supplied an unsourced substitute ('Keeping plants spaced for airflow and not overwatering keeps lavender vigorous enough to shrug off minor pests'). The first half is REFUTED by two T1 sources that each publish a specific prevention step, and the second half connects lavender spacing and irrigation to spittlebug pressure, which no document read states; spacing and airflow are sourced for FOLIAR FUNGAL pathogens on this crop, not for this insect.
prevention_seasoned.anchor: uc_ipm -- 'Cut spittlebug-infested weeds in the spring before the insects mature and spread.' (https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/spittlebugs/); umn_ext -- 'Remove weeds near your gardens' (https://extension.umn.edu/yard-and-garden-insects/spittlebugs)

prevention_beginner.new: Clear the weeds around the planting in spring. Spittlebugs build up on nearby weeds and move onto lavender from there, so cutting weedy patches while the insects in them are still young is the step that actually prevents them.
prevention_beginner.why: Same defect as prevention_seasoned: 'Nothing special is needed' is refuted, and the vigor-and-spacing sentence that followed it is an unsourced template claim reused across crops.
prevention_beginner.anchor: uc_ipm -- 'Cut spittlebug-infested weeds in the spring before the insects mature and spread.'; umn_ext -- 'Remove weeds near your gardens'

cause_seasoned.new: Spittlebug nymphs, which shelter inside their own foam while feeding on plant sap. The damage is mostly cosmetic on an established plant, though the foam masses are occasionally abundant, and a shoot tip that has been fed on may grow distorted.
cause_seasoned.why: 'Numbers are usually low' has no anchor and runs against the sources: UC IPM describes masses that are 'occasionally abundant'. Replaced with two facts the documents do carry, and the cosmetic-damage half is kept because all three sources support it.
cause_seasoned.anchor: uc_ipm -- "Spittlebugs' obvious and occasionally abundant masses of white foam on foliage and stems may be annoying, but they do not seriously harm established woody plants in landscapes."; rhs -- 'if the nymph has been feeding at the shoot tip, this may cause some distorted growth' (https://www.rhs.org.uk/biodiversity/cuckoo-spit-spittlebugs)

cause_beginner.new: Young spittlebugs hiding in the foam while they feed. They do little real harm, though you can find a lot of the froth at once in some years, and a shoot they have been feeding on may grow a little twisted.
cause_beginner.why: 'There are usually only a few' has no anchor and contradicts UC IPM's 'occasionally abundant masses'. The harmlessness half holds and is kept.
cause_beginner.anchor: uc_ipm -- 'occasionally abundant masses of white foam on foliage and stems may be annoying, but they do not seriously harm established woody plants'; rhs -- 'this may cause some distorted growth'

control_ladder.note_beginner: Look every new plant over for whiteflies before it comes into the garden. This is the first thing UC IPM tells you to do, because most whitefly problems arrive on a plant somebody carried home rather than flying in.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Inspect new plants for adults and for the nonmobile nymphs on the leaf undersides before they join the planting. It is the cheapest step available and the only one that acts before the pest is present, which on a long-lived perennial matters more than on an annual you will pull out in autumn.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Shiny metallic-coated paper or reflective plastic laid on the soil repels whiteflies, and it works best around small plants. Lay it on bare ground with the edges buried, and take it up when the plant gets large or the weather turns hot.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The published effect is repellent and it is strongest away from small plants, so on a perennial this belongs to the first season rather than to an established bush. Two removal rules ride with it and both are the source's own: take the mulch up when plants get large, and take it up when summer temperatures get high, to prevent overheating the plant. Clear the weeds off the bed before laying it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Prune out isolated infested leaves as soon as you first spot them. If the plant is already carrying a lot, taking off the most heavily loaded leaves is still worth doing: it can bring the numbers down far enough for the insects that eat whiteflies to handle the rest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Two separate uses, at two different stages. Early, prune out isolated infested leaves at first detection. Later, hand removal of leaves heavily infested with the nonmobile nymphal and pupal stages may reduce populations to levels that natural enemies can contain, which makes this the step that hands the problem to the predators rather than one that stops paying once the infestation is general.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep ants off the plant. Whiteflies produce honeydew, the honeydew draws ants, and the ants then drive off the insects that would otherwise eat the whiteflies for you.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Ants tending a honeydew source interfere with the natural enemies that do most of the control here, so excluding them protects the biological control rather than killing anything itself. UC IPM flags dust and ants together as the two things that most often disrupt whitefly natural enemies.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hose the adults off with a strong stream of water. Washing the foliage down also knocks off dust, and dusty leaves are part of what lets whitefly numbers climb.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Syringing dislodges adults, and it does a second job: hot, dry, dusty conditions favor whiteflies and inhibit their natural enemies. Note the crop-specific limit, because the source is written for gardens generally. Wash the FOLIAGE; do not answer a dust problem on lavender by watering the ground more, since sitting in wet soil is what gives this plant its one genuinely dangerous disease.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Yellow sticky traps catch flying adults, but they are better at telling you whether whiteflies are present and building than at controlling them. Set the sticky part level with where the insects are, and face it toward the plant but out of direct sun.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Treat these as monitoring first: the source is explicit that traps are most useful for detecting whiteflies rather than controlling them, and that they will not eliminate a damaging population. Whiteflies do not fly far, so useful numbers are high, quoted as one trap per medium-size vegetable plant and as many as one per two large plants. Keep the yellow surface level with the infestation, out of direct sunlight, and cleaned, or it stops catching anything.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lacewings, lady beetles and tiny parasitic wasps do most of the work on whiteflies, and outbreaks usually follow something disturbing them. Do not spray when they are around, and keep dust down, because dust kills them too.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Outbreaks frequently occur when natural enemies are disturbed or destroyed by pesticides, dust buildup, or ants, so conserving them is the center of this program and not a courtesy. Avoiding insecticides that kill natural enemies is described by the source as a very important part of whitefly management. Parasitized nymphs show round or oval exit holes; a healthy whitefly leaves a T-shaped one, which is how you tell whether the wasps are already working.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Insecticidal soap is the last step and a limited one: it kills only the whiteflies the spray actually wets, so you need to cover the undersides of the infested leaves and repeat it. Use it only when the plant is not dry-stressed and the temperature is under 90°F, and spray the infested foliage rather than the flowers.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap and the oils alongside it control only those whiteflies directly sprayed, so thorough coverage and repeat applications are both required, and the leaves that need it most are the lowest and hardest to reach. The limits are the source's: not on drought-stressed plants, not above 90°F. Early evening, with enough light to apply safely but no direct sun on the plant, is the suggested window. Confine it to infested growth, since it kills the soft-bodied beneficials it wets and lavender in bloom is a pollinator plant.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Occasional small clusters of tiny white flying insects on new growth. Whiteflies are one of only four invertebrates UC IPM lists for lavender, and on this crop they read as an occasional find rather than a recurring problem.
symptoms_seasoned.why: Two defects. First, 'or soft aphids': the aphid half of this entry is unsupported across eight documents, and the omission looks deliberate, since UC IPM's host index lists Aphids on rosemary and omits them from lavender. Second, 'most likely on stressed or overcrowded plants in poor conditions rather than on healthy lavender' asserts a stress-susceptibility link that no document read makes for lavender.
symptoms_seasoned.anchor: ucanr_ext -- lavender host page, Pests and Disorders > Invertebrates lists exactly 'Leafhoppers', 'Spider Mites', 'Spittlebugs', 'Whiteflies' (https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/lavender/); ncsu_ext -- 'Few insect problems have been reported on field-grown lavender.'

symptoms_beginner.new: Every so often, a few tiny white flies on the new growth. Lavender gets very few insect pests, and this is one of the minor ones.
symptoms_beginner.why: 'or small soft bugs' is the aphid half, unsupported. 'usually only on plants that are stressed or too crowded' is the same unsourced stress link as in symptoms_seasoned.
symptoms_beginner.anchor: ucanr_ext -- lavender host page invertebrate list; wsu_ext_lavender_prcr -- 'Lavender has few pests and diseases.' (https://ppo.puyallup.wsu.edu/lavender/)

organic_treatment_seasoned.new: Rinse them off with water or use insecticidal soap if numbers climb. Lavender is a low-input crop by reputation and few insect problems have been reported on it, so treat a whitefly find as a one-off rather than the start of a spray program.
organic_treatment_seasoned.why: The second sentence, 'Removing nearby stressors and improving airflow usually resolves it', has no anchor: nothing read connects airflow or stress relief to whitefly pressure on lavender. Replaced with the entry's best-anchored material. The first sentence is RETAINED and is now properly anchored: I first refused this entry's ladder because UC IPM Pest Note 7401 had not been read, and the orchestrator then read it on 2026-09-04. It publishes both halves of that sentence, so what the record pass filed as anchorable-but-unread is anchored.
organic_treatment_seasoned.anchor: uc_ipm -- 'Hose adults off plants with a strong stream of water.' and 'Most less-toxic products such as insecticidal soaps, neem oil, or petroleum-based oils control only those whiteflies that are directly sprayed.' (https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/whiteflies/, read directly 2026-09-04); wsu_ext_lavender_prcr -- 'Lavender has few pests and diseases. It is often promoted as a sustainable crop because growers do not commonly need to apply pesticides and fertilizers in its production.'; ncsu_ext -- 'Few insect problems have been reported on field-grown lavender.'

organic_treatment_beginner.new: Spray them off with water, or use insecticidal soap if there are a lot. Lavender rarely needs spraying at all, so this is a one-off, not a routine.
organic_treatment_beginner.why: 'Giving the plant more air and removing stress usually fixes it' has no anchor for this pest on this crop. The water-and-soap sentence is retained and is now anchored at UC IPM Pest Note 7401, read 2026-09-04.
organic_treatment_beginner.anchor: uc_ipm -- 'Hose adults off plants with a strong stream of water.' and soaps and oils 'control only those whiteflies that are directly sprayed'; wsu_ext_lavender_prcr -- 'growers do not commonly need to apply pesticides and fertilizers in its production'

prevention_seasoned.new: Inspect any new plant for whiteflies before it enters the garden, keep ants off the plants, since ants protect whiteflies from the insects that eat them, and hold off on broad sprays while natural enemies are present. Skip heavy organic mulches such as sawdust or wood chips around the crowns, which are reported on this crop to raise both fungal and insect problems; one to two inches of white sand is the mulch recommended for lavender instead.
prevention_seasoned.why: Two defects, one of them mine. First, the original 'Vigorous, unstressed lavender rarely attracts these pests' asserts a vigor-to-pest-pressure link no document read makes. Second, my own first replacement imported 'full sun, light sharply drained ground, 2 to 3 feet apart' into a whitefly entry. That is NC State's spacing-for-air-circulation claim, published against LEAF SPOT, and I had already pulled the identical claim out of the Phytophthora entry for being attached to the wrong problem. Applying that rule in one place and not the other was inconsistent, so the siting and spacing are gone and the cell now carries UC IPM's actual whitefly prevention plus the one lavender-specific insect statement any read document publishes.
prevention_seasoned.anchor: uc_ipm -- 'Prevent whitefly problems by reducing dusty conditions, choosing less susceptible plants, using reflective mulches, and avoiding pesticides that kill whitefly natural enemies.' and 'Always inspect new plants for whiteflies and nymphs before introducing them in the greenhouse or garden.' and 'Keep ants out of plants since they protect whiteflies from natural enemies.' (https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/whiteflies/); ncsu_ext -- 'Avoid heavy organic mulches (sawdust, wood chips) as they can increase both fungal pathogens and insect problems.' and 'Dr. A. O. Tucker advises using one to two inches of white sand as a mulch around plants to reduce fungal pathogen infection.'

prevention_beginner.new: Check new plants for whiteflies before you bring them home, and keep ants out of the plant, because ants protect whiteflies from the insects that would otherwise eat them. Avoid piling wood chips or sawdust around the base; on lavender those heavy mulches are reported to bring more insect and fungal trouble, and a thin layer of white sand is the better choice.
prevention_beginner.why: 'Healthy plants rarely get these bugs' is the unsourced vigor-to-pest-pressure claim, and my first replacement carried over 'in full sun with room around it', which is the leaf-spot spacing claim on the wrong problem. Both gone; replaced with UC IPM's published whitefly prevention and NC State's mulch guidance.
prevention_beginner.anchor: uc_ipm -- 'Inspect new plants for whiteflies before bringing them into your garden.' and 'Keep ants out of plants since they protect whiteflies from natural enemies.'; ncsu_ext -- 'Avoid heavy organic mulches (sawdust, wood chips) as they can increase both fungal pathogens and insect problems.'

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lavender rots where the ground stays wet, so this one is decided by where you put the plant. Give it light, sharply drained soil in a dry, open, sunny position, water deeply but only once the top few inches have dried out, and never let water stand around the base.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Prolonged soil saturation and standing water at the base are the conditions the water molds need, so drainage is the control here and fungicides do not stand in for it. On heavy or low-lying ground, plant on a mound: UC IPM puts that at 8 to 10 inches for annuals and up to 2 feet with a gradual slope for a perennial. Let the top few inches dry thoroughly between waterings and keep soil and mulch off the crown itself.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Variety choice shifts the odds a little. Among lavender types, the big lavandin hybrids are reported to hold up better against the wilt diseases than English lavender, and cultivars with gray foliage or dark flowers are the most susceptible. Treat it as a hedge, not a way to grow lavender on wet ground.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Take a resistant variety where one is offered. The reported gradient runs lavandin over English lavender for the vascular wilts, with gray-foliage and dark-flowered cultivars at the susceptible end and pale-flowered types holding up better. NC State words that gradient for the wilt diseases, and its own pathogen list files Phytophthora spp. under wilt, so read it as tilting the odds on a site you have already drained, not as a substitute for draining it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Buy certified nursery stock and look the plant over before it goes in the ground. A rot that arrives in the pot has already skipped past every other step here.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Select certified nursery stock, and a resistant rootstock or variety where one is available. Root and crown rot has no in-ground rescue, so a plant that arrives already infected is a loss paid for at purchase; inspecting at the nursery costs nothing and is the last point at which the decision is entirely yours.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Dig out and get rid of a lavender whose crown has gone soft. It will not come back, and diseased tissue dropped on a compost pile can carry the problem on.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A substantial infection rarely recovers, so removing and destroying the affected plant is the honest response rather than a rescue attempt. Do not put a susceptible replacement in the same spot until the drainage that caused it has actually been fixed, since the ground, not the plant, is what failed.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Shoots wilt, brown, and die back, and unlike a plant that is simply dry it does not recover when you water it; whole shoots can die inside the bush while the outer growth turns pale green with its flowers drooping. Darkened areas often develop in the bark around the crown and the upper roots. It is the disease of concern for lavender, and it takes hold where the soil stays wet.
symptoms_seasoned.why: 'Yellowing' has no lavender anchor and is dropped. The crown sign was ALSO dropped in my first pass, as tree-scoped, and that was an over-correction which I am reversing on review. UC IPM 74133's 'Darkened areas in the bark around the crown and upper roots' describes WOODY tissue, and lavender is a woody subshrub, the same basis on which the record pass accepted UC IPM's 'established woody plants in landscapes' as on-host for this crop. Removing it left the reader with no sign separating this disease from drought, which on a plant grown deliberately dry is the distinction that matters, so the irrigation test is now stated explicitly alongside it. 'Gumming' is NOT carried: that is a stone-fruit and tree feature.
symptoms_seasoned.anchor: uc_ipm 74133 -- 'Unlike plants suffering from water stress, plants don't recover when irrigated.' and 'Darkened areas in the bark around the crown and upper roots often develop, sometimes with gumming.' (read directly 2026-09-04, https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/phytophthora-root-and-crown-rot/); wsu_ext_lavender_prcr -- image captions 'the interior shoots are all dead and the shoots around the outside are pale green with their flowers drooping'; ncsu_ext -- 'rapid wilting, browning, and dying of leaves and succulent shoots'

symptoms_beginner.new: The plant wilts, browns, and dies back even though the soil is wet, and watering more makes no difference, which is what separates it from a plant that is simply too dry. Whole shoots can die off while the rest of the bush looks pale and tired, and the bark at the base and on the upper roots often goes dark. It is the disease most likely to kill an established lavender, and it comes from ground that stays too wet.
symptoms_beginner.why: 'Leaves yellow' has no lavender anchor. 'This is the main disease that kills lavender' is a rank claim in tension with NC State's 'The most common disease problem with lavender is wilt', so it is softened. The dark base is RESTORED after review: I removed it in my first pass as tree-scoped, which over-corrected, since the source describes bark on woody plants and lavender is woody. The watering test is now stated, because it is the sign that tells this apart from drought.
symptoms_beginner.anchor: uc_ipm 74133 -- "Unlike plants suffering from water stress, plants don't recover when irrigated." and 'Darkened areas in the bark around the crown and upper roots often develop'; ncsu_ext_lavandula_angustifolia -- 'Root rot is caused by overwatering.'

cause_seasoned.new: Water mold pathogens that thrive in saturated, poorly drained soil and attack the roots and crown. Many Phytophthora species cause root and crown rot on their hosts, so this is a group of organisms rather than one, and prolonged saturation or standing water at the base is what lets them in.
cause_seasoned.why: 'Wet feet, not cold, is the underlying cause' is a rhetorical contrast no document read makes; it is the record asserting what the literature does not say. Replaced with the WSU statement about the genus and the UC IPM statement about saturation, both of which the entry needs and neither of which it carried.
cause_seasoned.anchor: wsu_ext_lavender_prcr -- 'Phytophthora species are microscopic organisms that cause disease in plants. Many species have been identified as the primary causes of root and crown rot of their host plants.'; uc_ipm -- 'Avoid prolonged saturation of the soil or standing water around the base'

cause_beginner.new: A rot that takes hold when soil stays soggy and drains badly, attacking the roots and base. It is caused by water molds, a group of soil organisms that need wet ground to spread and infect, so soil that never dries out is what sets it up.
cause_beginner.why: 'The real cause is wet soil, not cold weather' is the same unanchored contrast as in cause_seasoned.
cause_beginner.anchor: wsu_ext_lavender_prcr -- 'Many species have been identified as the primary causes of root and crown rot of their host plants.'; csu_ext_lavender_07245 -- 'Lavender has no major pests in Colorado but can develop root rot if drainage is insufficient.'

organic_treatment_seasoned.new: A plant with a substantial infection rarely recovers, so once the crown is rotting the realistic move is to remove and destroy it rather than nurse it. Everything that works here happens at the site and before planting, and a fungicide is not a substitute for drainage.
organic_treatment_seasoned.why: 'There is no cure' overstates UC IPM 74133's hedged 'rarely recovers' into an absolute, which is the safety-absolute pattern this pass exists to catch. Softened to the source's own wording, and the removal advice is kept because NC State does publish it.
organic_treatment_seasoned.anchor: uc_ipm -- 'A plant with a substantial Phytophthora infection rarely recovers.' and 'do not rely on pesticide applications alone to control Phytophthora root and crown rot diseases'; ncsu_ext -- 'If damaged plants are present, remove and destroy any infected plant material and avoid replanting with susceptible varieties.'

organic_treatment_beginner.new: A plant that far gone rarely comes back, so pull out affected plants and throw them away instead of trying to save them. The answer is preventing it with good drainage, not curing it.
organic_treatment_beginner.why: 'Once the base is rotting there is no fix' is the beginner-register form of the same overstated absolute.
organic_treatment_beginner.anchor: uc_ipm -- 'A plant with a substantial Phytophthora infection rarely recovers.'; ncsu_ext -- 'remove and destroy any infected plant material'

prevention_seasoned.new: Plant in sharply drained soil in full sun, water deeply but infrequently, and never let lavender sit in wet ground. On clay, plant on a raised bed or a mound with a gradual slope, keep the crown clear of soil and mulch, and start from certified nursery stock, taking a resistant variety where one is offered.
prevention_seasoned.why: 'and space plants for airflow' is attached to the wrong problem. Spacing is genuinely sourced on this crop, but for FOLIAR fungal pathogens by way of air circulation, and air circulation does nothing for a soilborne water mold attacking roots; it already appears correctly in the leaf-spot entry. Replaced with two prevention steps UC IPM does publish for this disease.
prevention_seasoned.anchor: uc_ipm -- 'The mounds should be 8 to 10 inches high for annuals and up to 2 feet high with a gradual slope for trees and perennials.' and 'Select certified nursery stock and resistant rootstocks or varieties when available.'; ncsu_ext -- air circulation and 2-3 ft spacing are given 'In order to discourage fungal pathogens', which is the leaf-spot claim, not this one

prevention_beginner.new: Plant in well-draining soil in full sun, water deeply but rarely, and never let lavender sit in soggy ground. On heavy clay, plant on a mound or a raised bed, keep soil and mulch pulled back from the base, and start with healthy nursery stock.
prevention_beginner.why: 'and give plants room' carries the same misattributed spacing claim as prevention_seasoned: spacing on this crop is sourced against leaf spot, not against a soilborne root and crown rot.
prevention_beginner.anchor: uc_ipm -- 'Select certified nursery stock and resistant rootstocks or varieties when available.' and the mound heights; usu_ext_english_lavender -- 'Do not overwater or let water stand around the plants.'

control_ladder.note_beginner: Set lavender 2 to 3 feet apart in a dry, open, sunny spot. Air moving freely through the planting is the main defense against leaf spot, and it is decided when you space the plants rather than later.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spacing at 2 to 3 feet on an open, sunny site is the published measure here, and NC State gives it for exactly this reason, to discourage fungal pathogens. Trimming the lower branches through the growing season is the in-season half of the same job: the base of a maturing bush is where the canopy closes over first.

control_ladder.note_beginner: One to two inches of white sand around the plants is the mulch recommended for lavender, and it is meant to cut fungal infection. Skip the heavy organic mulches such as wood chips and sawdust here, because on lavender they push fungal problems the other way.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: White sand at one to two inches is the lavender-specific recommendation, and a mineral layer over the soil surface is the barrier that keeps rain splash from carrying soil onto the lowest leaves. The heavy organic mulches are a documented contra-indication on this crop, reported to raise both fungal pathogens and insect problems, so the straw and wood-chip options that suit other crops do not transfer here.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Rake the fallen leaves out from under the bush and take off any foliage that is badly marked, rather than letting that litter sit there through the winter.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Stripping spotted foliage and clearing the litter beneath the plant lowers what is left to start the next round. This is general leaf-spot practice rather than a lavender-specific finding, and on a crop where the disease stays minor it belongs as a light habit, not a program.

unreachable_claims: SPITTLEBUG LADDER CAP (umn_ext): 'Pesticides are not effective' -- the spittle mass shields the nymph. This is the single most useful ladder fact for this problem and no method can carry it, because it is an instruction to STOP, not a control. It is why this ladder ends at physical with three rungs and reaches for neither soft_chemical nor conventional, even though six insect-reaching materials exist in the catalog.

ncsu_ext (New Crops), INSECT half: 'Avoid heavy organic mulches (sawdust, wood chips) as they can increase both fungal pathogens and insect problems.' The only insect-reaching mulch method is `reflective_mulch`, which is specifically silver reflective film that repels incoming winged adults, so hanging a heavy-mulch contra-indication on it would be bending a method rather than using it. Carried into `Whiteflies.prevention_beginner`/`prevention_seasoned` as prose instead. The FUNGAL half of the same sentence IS carried, on the leaf-spot `splash_barrier_mulch` rung.

wsu_ext_lavender_prcr, the diagnostic pathway: 'Diagnostic services are available from the WSU Plant and Insect Diagnostic Laboratory', plus a published do-it-yourself sampling guide for testing your own plants for PRCR. A real, lavender-specific monitoring step, and there is no method in the 64 for lab diagnosis or sampling. If a `diagnostic_confirmation` method is ever minted, lavender PRCR is a ready first citation.

uc_ipm PN 74133's conventional materials for Phytophthora on ornamentals (fosetyl-al / Aliette, phosphorous-acid products, mefenoxam). The catalog's only conventional fungicides are `chlorothalonil` and `mancozeb`, both `fungal_foliar` protectants, and neither is any of those actives. Naming one to fill the conventional tier would invent a recommendation, so no conventional rung was authored -- which also matches the source's own 'do not rely on pesticide applications alone'.

uc_ipm spittlebug natural enemies (birds, assassin bugs, parasitic wasps). `beneficial_predators` exists and reaches `insect`, but UC IPM states their importance is 'not well known', so a biological rung would assert more than the source does. Not authored; recorded here so the omission reads as a decision rather than an oversight.

Spittlebug overwintering site: uc_ipm says eggs sit 'on or in stems or needles', umn_ext says they 'can live through the winter in leaf litter'. The two T1 sources disagree, so no `garden_sanitation` rung was authored for this pest on a clear-the-debris rationale, which would have required picking a side silently.

uc_ipm whiteflies, 'choosing less susceptible plants' / 'Avoid or remove plants that repeatedly host high populations of whiteflies'. DECLINED on `resistant_varieties`, which was mechanically available (applies_to `any`). Read in full, the advice is to avoid or remove the HOST SPECIES, not to pick a cultivar, and no document read reports cultivar-level whitefly susceptibility in Lavandula. A `resistant_varieties` rung would tell a reader a whitefly-resistant lavender exists to buy; the only honest form of this advice is 'grow something else', which is not advice about lavender.

uc_ipm whiteflies, Encarsia: 'Encarsia spp parasites are commercially available for release in greenhouse situations; however, they are not generally recommended for outdoor use because they are not well adapted for survival in temperate zones.' `augmentative_release` is in the catalog and reaches `insect`, and this is a documented instruction NOT to use it in a garden. Recorded as a sourced decline rather than an omission.

uc_ipm whiteflies, the two end-of-season removal lines: 'Remove and destroy whitefly-infested vegetable plants after harvest' and 'Promptly destroy infested annuals when the flowering or fruiting period ends'. CORRECTION TO MY OWN VERIFICATION, because I reported a number that was too low. I first measured rung-note similarity with an n-gram PREFILTER, comparing each note only against corpus strings sharing a rare 6-gram, and reported a worst ratio of 0.515. The unscreened exhaustive run over all 13,997 shipped strings returns 0.585, on a pair my prefilter never looked at: Leaf spot / garden_sanitation / note_beginner against apricot's Shot hole garden_sanitation note. The prefilter was the defect. Two sanitation sentences about raking fallen leaves can be structurally similar while sharing no n-gram at all, so screening by shared n-grams cannot find the nearest neighbor by ratio, and a confident number came from my own screen rather than from the data. The pair itself is clean: zero shared 4-grams, 5-grams, 6-grams and 7-grams, and the resemblance is the practice, not the prose. difflib's asymmetry shows on it too, 0.553 one way and 0.585 the other, which is why the max of both orders is the figure. FINAL, exhaustive, unscreened: 36 rung notes, worst ratio 0.585, worst shared 6-gram count 3, zero identical strings. Trust that figure, not the 0.515.
